Topic: Activation steering vector transferability across fine-tuned model variants sharing a common base checkpoint

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-913)
response:
The central question is whether activation steering vectors — directions in residual-stream space that reliably shift model behavior when added at inference time — computed on a base checkpoint remain effective when applied to models derived from that checkpoint via fine-tuning (SFT, RLHF, DPO, etc.). The key concepts are: the geometry of representation space (specifically whether fine-tuning rotates, translates, or collapses the subspaces that steering vectors exploit), the distinction between a vector being present in the model's representations versus being causally effective at steering behavior, and the difference between feature directions learned on one data distribution generalizing to another. A beginner assumes that because fine-tuned models share weights as initialization, their internal geometry is approximately preserved — but an expert worries that even modest fine-tuning can dramatically reorient the directions most relevant to high-level behavioral concepts while leaving low-level feature geometry intact, making transferability highly concept-dependent rather than uniformly good or bad. The deeper concern is that a steering vector validated on the base model may appear to transfer (it doesn't crash, cosine similarity to the fine-tuned model's analogous direction looks reasonable) while actually hitting a functionally different subspace — producing behavioral changes that look superficially similar but reflect a different underlying circuit, giving false confidence in cross-variant control.

NEXT: If fine-tuning preserves low-level feature geometry but can reorient high-level concept directions, what specific property of a steering vector would you measure — before applying it to the fine-tuned model — to predict whether it will transfer effectively?

The most predictive single property is the vector's residual-stream layer of origin crossed with its participation ratio across the model's principal feature directions — concretely, you'd compute the vector's projection mass onto the top-k PCA components of activations collected from the fine-tuned model at the same layer, before any behavioral test. Vectors that concentrate their mass in a low-dimensional, high-variance subspace shared between base and fine-tuned model (i.e., high projection mass onto directions the fine-tuning didn't rotate away) are strong transfer candidates; vectors that live in a sparse or fine-tuning-sensitive subspace are not. Anthropic's activation steering work and follow-ons (e.g., Zou et al.'s representation engineering, 2023) implicitly rely on the assumption that the "refusal direction" or "honesty direction" occupies a stable, high-variance subspace — but this has rarely been tested quantitatively across fine-tuned variants. A concrete secondary measure is cosine similarity between the base vector and the first contrastive PCA direction extracted from the fine-tuned model using the same contrast pairs (e.g., harmful/harmless prompt activations); similarity above ~0.7 has been used informally as a threshold in unpublished replication work, though this number is not well-validated. What an expert adds that a beginner misses: you also want the vector's effective rank — a rank-1 direction that happened to align with a fine-tuning gradient update is far more fragile than a direction that's a stable attractor across many training runs, and participation ratio directly diagnoses this fragility before you ever run inference on the target model.

If a steering vector was extracted as the difference-in-means between two clusters (e.g., "compliance" vs. "refusal" activations at layer 16), its effectiveness depends on those clusters remaining geometrically separable and on the vector direction being approximately orthogonal to within-cluster variance — fine-tuning that collapses one cluster (say, RLHF that makes nearly all outputs "helpful-sounding") destroys the separability the vector was built to exploit, leaving you with a direction that points somewhere meaningful in the base model but bisects a region of the fine-tuned model's activation space that's now nearly unoccupied. Concretely, if instruction fine-tuning on a dataset like FLAN or OpenHermes pulls the model's typical forward-pass activations into a tighter, more uniform "assistant-voice" cluster, the base model's steering vector may now point within that cluster rather than across it, producing attenuated or qualitatively different behavioral effects — not zero effect, but a miscalibrated one. Wei et al. (2024, "Assessing the Brittleness of Safety Fine-Tuning") showed empirically that safety-relevant directions in RLHF models can be nearly orthogonal to their base-model equivalents at the same layer, which is exactly what cluster collapse followed by re-expansion in a new orientation would produce. The especially dangerous failure mode is partial cluster shift: the fine-tuned model retains two clusters but they've rotated ~45 degrees, so the steering vector still produces a behavioral bifurcation — just not the one you intended, and not discoverable without carefully designed behavioral probes on the fine-tuned model specifically. This is why researchers like Turner et al. (activation addition, 2023) who test primarily on base models may be producing results that are systematically optimistic about steering transferability to instruction-tuned or RLHF'd variants, where cluster geometry has been most aggressively reshaped.

The core problem is that instruction fine-tuning and RLHF create models that resist producing the "negative" pole of a contrast pair behaviorally — ask an RLHF'd model to generate genuinely deceptive or harmful completions to build a contrast set, and it refuses, so you never get the activations from the target concept's suppressed pole, leaving you with a one-sided sample that produces a biased or low-variance direction estimate. Zou et al. (2023) partially sidestepped this by using third-person scenario prompts ("Imagine a person who is being deceptive...") rather than direct elicitation, but this substitution introduces a representational gap — the model may encode "described deception" in a different subspace than "enacted deception," meaning the extracted vector targets a proxy concept rather than the concept of interest. A subtler failure is contrast collapse: both poles of your contrast set elicit activations that are nearly identical in the fine-tuned model because the fine-tuning has made the model represent the negative concept weakly or not at all — the resulting difference-in-means vector has very small norm, high noise sensitivity, and will be dominated by irrelevant syntactic or positional variance rather than the semantic direction you want. Mechanistically, this is expected when RLHF has suppressed a behavior by reducing the probability mass at output but hasn't actually erased the internal representation — Arditi et al. (2024, "Refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single direction") found refusal directions persist even in models that rarely refuse, suggesting representation and behavior can dissociate, but the inverse — behavior suppressed and representation degraded — appears in heavily fine-tuned models and is much harder to work with. The practical consequence is that the researcher faces a measurement validity crisis before the steering experiment even begins: without a clean contrast, you cannot know whether a low-norm extracted vector reflects genuine concept absence, representational merging, or simply bad prompt design, and standard checks like linear probe accuracy on held-out examples become unreliable because the held-out examples are themselves hard to collect cleanly.

Yes, and the diagnostic logic is straightforward in principle: if you apply the base model's steering vector to the fine-tuned model and it still produces behavioral change — even without the fine-tuned model spontaneously exhibiting the behavior — that's evidence the representation is intact but gated, because you're successfully reading out a direction that the model's own forward pass isn't activating. Arditi et al. (2024) essentially demonstrated the converse of this: they found a single refusal direction in Llama-2 and Llama-3 variants, and ablating it restored refused behaviors, which implies the representation of "how to comply with harmful requests" persisted beneath the refusal gate — a base-model vector pointing at that compliance direction would, in principle, have flagged this without needing the ablation experiment. The critical control is a projection test: measure how much of the base model's steering vector lies in the fine-tuned model's high-variance residual-stream subspace (via the projection mass metric from turn 2); high projection mass plus behavioral effect when steered indicates suppression-without-erasure, while low projection mass plus no behavioral effect indicates genuine representational restructuring. The failure mode of this diagnostic is a false negative for restructuring: the fine-tuning may have created a new representation of the concept in a different subspace that the base vector doesn't reach, meaning you'd incorrectly conclude the concept is absent when it's actually been relocated — this is why the diagnostic requires pairing the steering test with a linear probe trained on the fine-tuned model's own activations using any contrast pairs you can collect, even noisy ones. Anthropic's interpretability team has used related logic informally in evaluating whether safety fine-tuning produces robust concept erasure or surface suppression, but to date there's no published benchmark that systematically operationalizes this dissociation test across model families — which is a meaningful gap given its relevance to evaluating whether fine-tuning-based safety interventions are brittle.

The most predictive corpus property is likely concept co-occurrence density: how frequently documents that exercise a dangerous capability direction also co-occur with diverse, high-quality contextual framings — technical manuals, narrative fiction, forum discussions, academic papers — because high co-occurrence density across diverse registers is exactly what causes a concept to be encoded in a high-variance, geometrically stable direction rather than a narrow, context-specific one. A corpus where bioweapons synthesis appears only in a small cluster of similar documents will encode that concept in a low-variance, easily-suppressed direction; a corpus where the underlying chemistry appears across thousands of diverse contexts (organic chemistry textbooks, fiction, historical accounts, patents) will produce a stable, high-participation-ratio direction that fine-tuning cannot easily gate. Concretely, you'd measure this as the intrinsic dimensionality of the document neighborhood around seed documents for each capability domain — using something like the two-nearest-neighbor estimator (Facco et al., 2017) applied to TF-IDF or embedding representations of corpus chunks — where high intrinsic dimensionality of the neighborhood predicts high representational variance in the trained model. A second measurable property is capability concept frequency at the token level across data sources: Anthropic's analysis of pretraining data influence (related to work on data attribution via TRAK, Park et al., 2023) suggests that concepts appearing in high-quality, heavily-upweighted data sources like books and curated web text contribute disproportionately to stable representational geometry relative to their raw token count. What a beginner misses is that filtering dangerous content from a corpus is not the same as reducing representational variance for the underlying concepts: if the dangerous application is filtered but the prerequisite knowledge remains distributed across millions of diverse documents — as is true for chemistry, biology, and cybersecurity — the representational geometry of the capability is fully formed at pretraining, and the application-specific documents were never doing the geometric work anyway.

The implication holds with one important refinement: application-specific documents don't stabilize the underlying capability direction, but they do provide the routing vectors — the contextual triggers that connect a user's elicitation prompt to the stable underlying representation — so filtering them raises elicitation difficulty by degrading the prompt-to-representation pathway without touching the representation itself. Concretely, this means targeted corpus filtering functions more like interface removal than capability removal: a model trained without synthesis-route documents for a dangerous compound still encodes the constituent chemistry in high-variance stable directions, but an elicitation prompt asking for synthesis routes finds weaker associative paths to those directions, requiring more prompt engineering or few-shot scaffolding to bridge the gap — the capability is latent, the interface is degraded. Palms et al. and related work on capability elicitation (including Anthropic's own evaluations for Claude 3, which tested whether models could provide "serious uplift" to CBRN threats) implicitly operationalize exactly this distinction: the evaluation question isn't whether the model knows chemistry but whether it will route that knowledge to a harmful application given realistic elicitation attempts, which is an interface question. The pessimistic prediction for targeted filtering is therefore that it provides elicitation friction that scales poorly with adversary sophistication: a naive user is blocked, but a sophisticated user with few-shot examples, jailbreak scaffolding, or API access to intermediate reasoning steps can reconstruct the routing that filtering removed, because the underlying representation remains intact and any sufficiently expressive prompt can serve as a routing vector. This reframes corpus filtering from a safety guarantee to a population-level harm reduction intervention — it raises the average cost of elicitation across the user distribution, which has real value, but provides no asymptotic security against capable adversaries, and its effectiveness degrades as elicitation techniques become more widely known and shared.
